references.text: Psalm 65:8 speaks of God who stills the roaring of the seas and the waves, reflecting Jesus' power over the storm and waves in this text.
Psalm 89:10 praises the Lord as ruler over the raging sea, who calms the waves, paralleling Jesus' rebuke of the wind and water.
Psalm 104:7 describes the waters fleeing at God's command, which parallels how the storm ceased when Jesus threatened the wind and waves.
Psalm 107:28-29 describes sailors crying out to the Lord in distress, and He calms the storm and waves—a clear parallel to the disciples crying out to Jesus, who then calmed the storm.
Jonah 1:4-6 describes a similar situation where Jonah sleeps during a storm while those on board fear for their lives and wake him, paralleling how the disciples woke Jesus during the storm.
Matthew 8:24-26 is the parallel account of this narrative in Matthew, where Jesus calms the sea after the disciples wake Him in fear.
Mark 4:37-39 is the parallel passage in Mark, recounting the same story of Jesus calming the storm after being awakened by the disciples.
Psalm 46:2-3 speaks of not fearing even if the earth gives way and mountains fall into the sea, thematically reflecting the lack of faith the disciples showed during the storm.
Isaiah 50:2 asks whether the Lord's hand is too short to save, mentioning His power to dry up the sea with a command—paralleling Jesus' rebuke of the water.
Nahum 1:4 describes the Lord threatening the sea and drying it up, reflecting Jesus' divine authority over natural forces in this text.
Luke 5:5 is the first time the disciples address Jesus as 'Epistata' (Master) in Luke, and the same title is used here by the frightened disciples.
